newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Crushing defeat for Afghan who kept changing sides.
newsitem.headline: Crushing defeat for Afghan who kept changing sides.

text.p: General Abdul Rashid Dostum, who lost the capital of his fiefdom in northern Afghanistan to the turbanned Islamic Taleban warriors on Saturday, had managed to survive by switching allegiance again and again during years of war.

He rose to power under the Soviet-backed government of Afghanistan in the 1980s as a leader of a militia composed mostly of fellow minority Uzbeks, who won a fierce reputation as the communist regime's troubleshooters, pacifying areas other units feared to enter.
When the government of communist President Najibullah was surrounded and struggling for survival in 1992, the security of Kabul was put into Dostum's hands.

Just as the United Nations were about to implement a power-sharing deal in April 1992, Dostum changed sides. He came to an agreement with one of the anti-communist guerrilla parties -- the Jamiat-i-Islami of Burhanuddin Rabbani -- to hand over Kabul to them.

Dostum's men then stopped President Najibullah from boarding a U.N. plane to leave the country. Najibullah spent four years under effective arrest in a U.N. compound in Kabul until the Taleban captured the city last September, seized the former president and hanged him.
Dostum established himself as leader of most of northern Afghanistan, in alliance with Rabbani against the rival guerrillas of Gulbuddin Hekmatyar's Hezb-i-Islami group.

But the relationship between Rabbani and Dostum soured and on January 1 1994, the general changed sides and joined Hekmatyar. An intense four-month battle broke out, in which Dostum was the main loser.

He retreated to Mazar-i-Sharif in the north of the country where he set up a parallel administration with its own money, foreign ministry, and increasingly strong ties with the former Soviet states of central Asia, which saw him as a bulwark against the Islamic movements that had defeated the Soviet army in Afghanistan.

He enjoyed being driven round his territory in a black Cadillac, followed by a convoy of Japanese four wheel drive vehicles, an armoured personnel carrier and two truck-mounted anti-aircraft batteries.

Dostum ran his military operations from the Qalai Jangir, a fort with crenellated 30-foot (10-metre) thick mud walls in Mazar--i-Sharif, and kept a carefully-guarded executive jet on the tarmac at the city's airport.

In contrast to the rule of Islamic guerrillas in Kabul to the south, Dostum's was relatively liberal, if equally lawless. His capital prospered on goods smuggled from the former Soviet Union to other parts of Afghanistan and its neighbours.

When Kabul fell to the militantly Islamic Taleban last year, Dostum became the senior partner in an anti-Taleban alliance consisting of his troops, those of the ousted Rabbani government, and the mainly Shi'ite Hezb-i-Wahdat party.
The alliance was always weak. All the partners had at one time fought each other, and there was little trust despite the threat of annihilation by the Taleban.
The seeds of Dostum's downfall were sown when one of his major commanders and a potential challenger for his power, Rasool Pahlawan, was assassinated in Mazar-i-Sharif last year.

Pahlawan's brother, Dostum's foreign minister General Abdul Malik, then took over command of his brother's forces. On Monday, Malik and 4,000 of his men defected to the Taleban in a move that echoed that of Dostum himself when he deserted President Najibullah.
Without Malik, who was pivotal in the defence of Dostum's northern fiefdom, the front line lbroke. On Saturday afternoon Mazar-i-Sharif fell to the Taleban.
Portraits of the general that had hung all over the city were used for target practice by jubilant young Taleban fighters.
Dostum has reportedly fled to neighbouring Uzbekistan, one of his staunchest supporters in his struggle against the Taleban.
